topic: Tense combinations — one situation, different tenses

cards.title: Past Simple — Past Continuous — Past Perfect
cards.subtitle: the same situation told three ways

items.sentence: Last Monday, Lisa and her husband fed the children when he came home.
items.note: Her husband came home and then they fed the children together. The past simple is used for actions which happened immediately one after the other in the past.

items.sentence: Last Tuesday, Lisa was feeding the children when her husband came home.
items.note: She was still feeding the children when her husband came home. The past continuous is used for a past action which was in progress when another action interrupted it.

items.sentence: Last Friday, Lisa had already fed the children when her husband came home.
items.note: She fed the children first. Her husband came home afterwards. The past perfect is used for an action which happened before another past action.

cards.title: Note the difference
cards.subtitle: Past Perfect and Past Simple after when

items.note: Tim had left before his sister phoned.
His sister phoned and then Tim left.

examples: a) in predictions about the future, usually with think, believe, be afraid, probably. I believe life will change in the 21st century.
b) for on-the-spot decisions or offers. It's late. I'll take a taxi home. I'll lend you my car if you want.
c) for actions, events or situations which will definitely happen in the future and which we cannot control. Winter will set in early this year.
d) for promises, threats, warnings, requests, hopes. Stop talking or I'll send you out of the class.
a) for plans, intentions or ambitions. I'm going to buy a sports car.
b) in predictions when there is evidence that something will happen in the near future. Someone's going to fall over that box if you don't move it.
for fixed arrangements in the near future. He's flying to Turkey next month. He has already booked his flight.
for timetables and programmes. The ferry leaves at eight o'clock tomorrow morning.
a) for actions which will be in progress at a stated future time. This time next week he'll be flying to Morocco.
b) for actions which will definitely happen as a result of a routine or arrangement. I'll be seeing Jim at work later on today.
c) when we ask politely about someone's plans for the near future. Will you be going to the dentist this afternoon?
for actions which will be finished before a stated future time. We will have returned home by Sunday afternoon.
to emphasise the duration of an action up to a certain time in the future. By the end of this week, she will have been working here for six years.

cards.title: Future forms — note
cards.subtitle: four rules that decide the form

items.case: We use the Present Continuous rather than be going to for things which are definitely arranged to happen in the future
examples: They're having a party next week.
They're going to have a party in two weeks.
items.hint: It's all arranged, the invitations have already been sent. — They've decided but it hasn't been arranged yet.

items.case: We use the Present Simple for timetables, programmes, etc.
examples: Our plane leaves at 10:30 am.

items.case: We do not use the Future tense after while, before, until, as soon as, if (conditional) and when (time conjunction)
examples: Call me when you arrive.
BUT When will you be ready?
items.hint: We can use when + will if when is a question word.

items.case: With the verbs go and come we often use the Present Continuous rather than be going to
examples: I'm going out tonight.
RATHER THAN I'm going to go out tonight.

cards.title: Future Perfect and time clauses
cards.subtitle: what tense goes after by the time, until, before

items: After the time expressions by the time, until, before we use the present simple, because they introduce time clauses. The future perfect and the future perfect continuous may come either before or after the time clause.

items.sentence: I will have tidied up by the time you get back.
items.note: The main clause is in the future perfect, the time clause after 'by the time' is in the present simple.

items.sentence: By the time she finishes work, we will have been waiting for more than an hour.
items.note: The time clause comes first and is still in the present simple; the main clause is in the future perfect continuous.

items.v: by, by the time, before, until, by then
